entries.question: When did the cursed fig tree die?
entries.summary: Matthew 21:19-20 says the fig tree 'presently' withered after Jesus cursed it, and the disciples marveled at the speed: 'How soon is the fig tree withered away!' Mark 11:13-14, 20-21 has the disciples observe the cursed tree only the *next morning*, withered from the roots — and Peter has to remind Jesus what he said the day before. Matthew's tree dies instantly; Mark's takes overnight.
entries.commentary: This pairs directly with the previous contradiction (id 450) on the *order* of the cursing and the temple cleansing. Once Matthew collapses Mark's two-day intercalated sequence into a single-event narrative, the timing of the tree's death gets compressed too. In Mark the natural reading is: day one, Jesus curses the tree on the way into Jerusalem; day two, walking back from Bethany, the disciples notice it has withered overnight. In Matthew, since the cursing and the discovery are part of the same scene, the tree has to die immediately — *parachrēma*, 'at once.' Davies and Allison flag this as one of Matthew's most obvious editorial intensifications of Mark's miracle traditions. Matthew does this elsewhere: in Matt 8:13 the centurion's servant is healed *in that hour* (Luke 7:10 just has him healed when the messengers return); in Matt 9:22 the hemorrhaging woman is healed *from that hour* (Mark 5:29 has her flow dry *immediately* but Matthew adds the formal time marker). The pattern is Matthean redactional intensification: miracles get faster and more dramatic. The apologist harmonization is that Matthew is telescoping — the withering happened overnight as Mark says, but Matthew compresses the timeline for narrative impact. Archer and Blomberg both run a version of this. The harmonization concedes the editorial point: the gospels do not record events in the same time-scale, and one or both authors are shaping the chronology for effect. Bart Ehrman in *Jesus, Interrupted* uses this exact pericope as a case study: the contradiction isn't a manuscript glitch, it's the result of two authors with different storytelling priorities. Steel-manning the telescoping defense: yes, ancient writers compressed events all the time. But that means at least one of these accounts is not a chronological transcript — which is the contradiction the question is asking about.

answers.answer_explanation:
And seeing a fig tree afar off having leaves, he came, if
				          haply he might find any thing thereon: and when he came to it, he
				          found nothing but leaves; for the time of figs was not yet. And Jesus answered and said
				          unto it, No man eat fruit of thee hereafter for ever. And his
				          disciples heard it. ... And in the morning, as they passed by, they
				          saw the fig tree dried up from the roots. And Peter calling to
				          remembrance saith unto him, Master, behold, the fig tree which thou
				          cursedst is withered away. Mark 11:13-14, 20-21

commentary_out.commentary:
This entry is the temporal twin of contradiction 450, which concerns the *order* of the cursing and the temple cleansing; here the issue is the *speed* of the tree's death. Matthew 21:19-20 has the tree wither 'presently' (παραχρῆμα, 'immediately, at once') the moment Jesus speaks, and the disciples marvel on the spot: 'How soon is the fig tree withered away!' Mark 11:13-14, 20-21 splits the cursing (day two) from the discovery (day three): only 'in the morning, as they passed by,' do the disciples see the tree 'dried up from the roots,' and Peter has to remind Jesus of the curse uttered the previous day. Matthew's tree dies in real time; Mark's withers overnight and unobserved.

The mechanism is the same redactional move analyzed in 450. Because Matthew dismantles Mark's intercalation and folds the cursing and the discovery into one continuous scene, the withering has to be instantaneous — there is no longer an intervening night for it to occur off-stage. The compression of order forces the compression of timing. Davies and Allison identify this as one of Matthew's clearest intensifications of Markan miracle material, and the tendency is documented across his Gospel. In Matt 8:13 the centurion's servant is healed 'in that hour' (ἐν τῇ ὥρᾳ ἐκείνῃ), where Luke 7:10 simply reports him well when the messengers return. In Matt 9:22 the hemorrhaging woman is healed 'from that hour' (ἀπὸ τῆς ὥρας ἐκείνης), where Mark 5:29 has the flow dry up 'immediately' (εὐθύς). The comparison is not a one-for-one word-swap — Matthew radically abbreviates the whole pericope, dropping most of Mark's detail — and the added 'from that hour' is best read as part of that same summarizing, result-focused tendency rather than a clause Matthew lifted and intensified. But the direction of travel is consistent: under Matthew's hand, miracles become tidier and more emphatically instantaneous, the time-markers heightening the wonder.

The apologetic harmonization is telescoping: Matthew compresses a process that, per Mark, took overnight, narrating its result without the intervening interval. Archer and Blomberg both defend this, and it is descriptively accurate — telescoping is a recognized feature of ancient narrative, and Matthew's παραχρῆμα can be read as marking the certainty rather than the literal instantaneity of the result. Steel-manned, the defense holds that no ancient reader expected wooden chronological precision and that summarizing a result is not falsifying it. Granting all that, the harmonization still concedes the substance of the contradiction: Matthew and Mark do not present the withering on the same time-scale, and Matthew's telescoping is itself the admission that he has shaped the chronology for narrative effect. Bart Ehrman uses this very pericope as a teaching case precisely because the divergence is not a manuscript corruption — the Greek text is stable — but the product of two evangelists with different storytelling priorities, visible the moment the parallels are read side by side. That is the methodological payoff: the difference is editorial, not scribal, and it cannot be dissolved without conceding that at least one account compresses the timeline. Verdict: harmonizable as Matthean telescoping, but only by granting that the two accounts report different time-scales for the same event.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The discrepancy resolves as Matthean telescoping: once Matthew collapses Mark's two-day intercalated sequence into a single scene, the withering necessarily appears instantaneous, an editorial intensification rather than a factual claim that can be reconciled with Mark's overnight timing. The harmonization works only by granting that Matthew compresses the chronology for dramatic effect, so the two accounts do not report the same time-scale.

entries.question: Should we do what the Pharisees say to do?
entries.summary: Matthew 23:1-3 has Jesus tell the crowds that because the scribes and Pharisees 'sit in Moses' seat,' the listeners should 'observe and do' whatever the Pharisees tell them — just don't imitate their behavior. Matthew 16:12, by contrast, has the disciples finally understand Jesus' warning that they should beware 'the doctrine of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees.' Same gospel, two opposite instructions about whether to follow Pharisaic teaching.
entries.commentary: This is one of the most internally tangled passages in Matthew, and even friendly commentators concede there's a real tension here. The Matt 23:2-3 saying is unique to Matthew — no parallel in Mark or Luke — and it sits at the head of a chapter that then proceeds to lambast the Pharisees in the harshest terms anywhere in the gospels ('woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites,' seven times). Davies and Allison in the ICC wrestle with this for several pages and conclude that 23:2-3 is best understood as a piece of inherited Matthean tradition the evangelist did not fully integrate, possibly reflecting an earlier stratum where Jesus' Jewish-Christian followers still operated within Pharisaic authority structures. Anthony Saldarini's *Matthew's Christian-Jewish Community* runs this line in detail: the saying reflects a community still legally Jewish, still under Pharisaic juridical authority, even as it is in bitter polemical conflict with Pharisaic leadership. So historically the contradiction reflects two layers of Matthean community life. The apologist harmonization is that Jesus was telling his audience to obey the Pharisees *only when* the Pharisees taught Mosaic law correctly — the 'sit in Moses' seat' qualifier limits the command to legitimate Torah interpretation, and Matt 16:12's warning about 'doctrine' refers to the Pharisees' *additional* teaching, their 'tradition of the elders.' That works as a logical reconciliation but it requires inserting a qualifier ('only when they teach Moses faithfully') that the text itself doesn't supply. Mark Allan Powell's argument that 23:3's 'observe and do' really means 'observe what they observe' — that is, watch their practice — is grammatically possible but most translators reject it. Ulrich Luz in Hermeneia treats the verse as an unresolved fossil. Steel-man: Matthew may be distinguishing positional authority (the seat) from personal authority (the men), and telling readers to respect the office while ignoring the officeholders. That distinction works for institutional theology but not as a coherent halakhic instruction.

answers.answer_explanation:
Then spake Jesus to the multitude, and to his disciples, Saying ... 
				whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do. Matthew 23:1-3

He [Jesus] bade them not beware of the leaven of bread, but of the doctrine of the Pharisees 
				and of the Sadducees. Matthew 16:12

commentary_out.commentary:
Few passages expose the seams of Matthew's redactional work as plainly as the collision between 23:2-3 and 16:12. In 23:1-3 Jesus tells the crowds and disciples that because the scribes and Pharisees 'sit on Moses' seat' (epi tes Mouseos kathedras ekathisan), they should do and observe (poiesate kai tereite) whatever the Pharisees tell them, while refusing to imitate their conduct. In 16:12 the disciples are finally said to grasp that Jesus had warned them to beware 'the teaching (didache) of the Pharisees and Sadducees.' The same evangelist thus records both an injunction to obey Pharisaic instruction and a warning against it.

The Matt 23:2-3 logion is unique to Matthew, with no Markan or Lukan parallel, and it stands as a jarring preface to the most savage anti-Pharisaic polemic in the canon, the sevenfold 'woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites' that follows. Davies and Allison devote several pages of the ICC to the problem and conclude that 23:2-3 is most plausibly inherited tradition the evangelist did not fully assimilate to his own viewpoint, a fossil from an earlier stratum in which Jesus' Jewish-Christian followers still functioned within Pharisaic juridical structures. Anthony Saldarini developed this into a full thesis: Matthew's community remained legally Jewish, still subject to Pharisaic authority in matters of Torah observance, even while locked in bitter polemical rivalry with Pharisaic leadership. J. Andrew Overman and David Sim situate the same Gospel within 'formative Judaism,' a sectarian movement competing for the same constituency, which accounts for how a single text can both defer to and denounce its rivals. On this reading the contradiction is not a logical lapse so much as a sedimentary record of two phases of community life lying side by side.

The principal harmonization, defended in conservative commentaries such as Hagner's WBC and Blomberg's NAC, distinguishes the *content* of legitimate Torah teaching from the Pharisees' additional rulings. On this view, when the Pharisees correctly expound Moses from the 'seat,' they are to be obeyed; 16:12's 'teaching' refers to their supplementary halakhah, the 'tradition of the elders' that 15:1-9 has Jesus reject for nullifying the commandment of God. This is a coherent reconciliation and deserves its hearing, but it works only by importing a limiting clause the text never states. Matt 23:3 says 'all things whatsoever' (panta hosa) they tell you, not 'all things they rightly derive from Moses.' Mark Allan Powell offered a different route, arguing that the 'seat of Moses' was a literal synagogue chair from which Torah was read aloud, so that 'whatever they tell you' means 'whatever Moses, through their reading, commands' rather than the Pharisees' own rulings; he even proposes that 'observe and do' be read as 'watch and do as they observe.' The reading is grammatically conceivable and archaeologically suggestive, but most translators and commentators reject the strained sense it requires of poiesate kai tereite. Ulrich Luz in Hermeneia simply treats the verse as an unresolved tension Matthew left standing.

A further steel-manning move distinguishes positional from personal authority: readers are to respect the office (the seat) while disregarding the unworthy officeholders, much as Christian tradition later distinguished the validity of an office from the sanctity of its holder. As institutional theology this is intelligible, but as a halakhic instruction it founders, because 16:12 warns precisely against the *teaching*, not merely the behavior, of the Pharisees, and 23:3 already separates teaching from behavior by telling hearers to obey the words while shunning the deeds. The two texts cannot be made to speak with one voice without an interpretive supplement neither supplies. Verdict: partially harmonizable, but most economically explained as an unintegrated layer in Matthew's Christian-Jewish tradition.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The tension softens if Matt 23:2-3 is read as endorsing legitimate Torah interpretation from the 'seat of Moses' while 16:12's warning targets the Pharisees' supplementary halakhah ('tradition of the elders'); but the qualifier 'only when they teach Moses faithfully' is supplied by the interpreter, not the text, so the resolution is incomplete and most critical scholars treat 23:2-3 as an unintegrated tradition.

entries.question: Did Jesus drink on the cross?
entries.summary: John 19:29-30 has Jesus receive the vinegar from the sponge and then declare "It is finished." Mark 15:23 has Jesus refuse the wine mingled with myrrh. Matthew 27:34 has Jesus taste the vinegar mingled with gall and refuse to drink. The Synoptic Jesus refuses the offered drink; the Johannine Jesus drinks it.
entries.commentary:
This contradiction is partly resolvable by distinguishing two separate drink-offers in the crucifixion sequence, but only partly. Mark 15:23 and Matthew 27:34 describe an offer of drugged wine before crucifixion — Mark calls it wine mingled with myrrh, Matthew shifts the substance to vinegar mingled with gall (apparently echoing Psalm 69:21). This pre-crucifixion offer was likely a Jewish custom of providing an analgesic to the condemned, and Jesus refuses to dull his suffering.

Mark 15:36 and Matthew 27:48 then describe a second, later offer near the moment of death — a sponge of vinegar (sour wine, oxos in Greek, the cheap wine of Roman soldiers) lifted to Jesus' lips. Mark and Matthew don't specify whether Jesus drank this second offering. John 19:28-30 jumps directly to this second offer and has Jesus actively receive the vinegar.

So the partial harmonization works: there are two distinct offers, and the Synoptic refusal applies to the first while the Johannine acceptance applies to the second. Carson, Morris, and Blomberg all make this move and it holds up textually.

Where the harmonization gets thin is the question of whether Jesus drinks the second offering in the Synoptics. Mark and Matthew don't explicitly say. John says yes. So strictly speaking, only John makes a positive claim about Jesus drinking. The Synoptics neither confirm nor deny the second drink. The contradiction at the SAB level — "did Jesus drink on the cross" — yields a Synoptic "no" only if you fold the first offer (clearly refused) into the question, and ignore that the second offer is silent in the Synoptics on whether he drank.

The more interesting critical-scholarly point, in Brown's Death of the Messiah, is that John has reshaped the vinegar scene to fulfill Psalm 69:21 explicitly — "in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink" — by adding the hyssop branch and the "I thirst" cry, neither of which appears in the Synoptics. John's account is theologically elaborated. The contradiction is real if you read the question as "did Jesus consume the drink offered to him," with the Synoptic answer being ambiguous to negative and the Johannine answer being affirmative.

answers.answer_explanation:
Now there was set a vessel full of vinegar: and they filled a spunge with vinegar, and put it
				    upon hyssop, and put it to his mouth. When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed 
				    his head, and gave up the ghost. John 19:29-30

And they gave him to drink wine mingled with myrrh: but he received it not. Mark 15:23
				        
				       They gave him vinegar to drink mingled with gall: and when he had tasted thereof, he would not
				    drink. Matthew 27:34

commentary_out.commentary:
The contradiction is real at the level of the bald question 'did Jesus drink on the cross?' but it is substantially defused once the crucifixion narratives are recognized to contain two separate drink-offers, distinguished by timing and by the substance offered.

The first offer comes before the crucifixion. Mark 15:23 reports oinos esmyrnismenos, 'wine mingled with myrrh'; Matthew 27:34 alters this to oxos meta choles, 'vinegar/sour wine mixed with gall.' Mark's myrrhed wine fits a known custom of providing an analgesic to the condemned; the Babylonian Talmud (b. Sanhedrin 43a) preserves a tradition that a stupefying drink was given to those led out to execution. Jesus refuses it in both Gospels — in Mark flatly ('he received it not'), in Matthew after tasting ('he would not drink'). Matthew's substitution of 'gall' is almost certainly an assimilation to Psalm 69:21 LXX ('they gave me gall for my food'), a redactional move Davies and Allison document. The refusal carries theological weight: Jesus declines to dull his suffering.

The second offer comes near the moment of death. Mark 15:36 and Matthew 27:48 describe a bystander filling a sponge with oxos — the cheap sour wine (posca) of Roman soldiers, not the same drink as the first offer — and lifting it on a reed to Jesus' lips. Crucially, the Synoptics do not say whether Jesus drank this. John 19:28-30 narrates only this second offer, prefaced by Jesus' cry 'I thirst' (dipso), and states that Jesus 'received' (elaben) the sour wine before declaring 'It is finished.'

The two-offer harmonization, defended by Carson, Morris, and Blomberg, is textually sound: the Synoptic refusal applies to the analgesic, the Johannine acceptance to the soldiers' posca, and there is no formal contradiction. Where the harmonization thins is the precise SAB question. Only John makes the positive assertion that Jesus drank; the Synoptics are simply silent on whether he consumed the second offering. So the cleanest statement is that the Synoptics record a refused first drink and an unresolved second drink, while John records an accepted second drink. The conflict arises only if one collapses both Synoptic offers into a single 'no.'

The more significant critical observation, developed at length in Brown's Death of the Messiah, is redactional rather than chronological. John has visibly reshaped the second offer to fulfill Psalm 69:21 explicitly. He adds the 'I thirst' saying (dipso), which has no Synoptic parallel, and he introduces a botanical oddity — the sour wine is raised on hyssop (hyssopos) rather than the reed (kalamos) of Mark and Matthew. Hyssop is a small, floppy plant ill-suited to lifting a sponge to a crucified man's mouth; many scholars suspect either a deliberate Passover allusion (hyssop applied the Passover blood in Exod 12:22, and John frames Jesus as the Passover lamb) or a textual corruption of hysso ('on a javelin'), a conjecture noted in the apparatus. Either way, John's scene is theologically elaborated to present Jesus as consciously fulfilling Scripture: 'that the scripture might be fulfilled, [he] saith, I thirst' (19:28).

Steel-manned, the apologetic case is strong on the surface contradiction and weak on the redactional one: it correctly shows that no verse states both that Jesus drank and that he refused the *same* offer, but it does not explain John's distinctive 'I thirst,' the hyssop, and the explicit fulfillment formula, which mark John's account as a deliberate theological composition rather than independent corroboration. Verdict: harmonizable as to the bare facts (two offers); the residual issue is Johannine theological elaboration, not factual contradiction.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: There are two distinct drink-offers in the crucifixion sequence: a pre-crucifixion analgesic wine (Mark 15:23 / Matt 27:34, refused) and a later sour-wine offer near death (Mark 15:36 / Matt 27:48 / John 19:29-30). The Synoptic refusal and the Johannine acceptance attach to different offers, so they do not directly conflict — but only John positively states Jesus drank, leaving the Synoptic second offer unresolved.

entries.question: How old was Abraham when he left Haran?
entries.summary: Genesis 12:4 says Abram was 75 years old when he departed Haran. Genesis 11:26 says Terah was 70 when he begat Abram; Genesis 11:32 says Terah died at 205. Acts 7:2-4 explicitly says Abraham left Haran only after Terah died. Doing the arithmetic — 205 minus 70 — Terah died when Abram was 135. The Genesis 11 chronology combined with Stephen's speech in Acts is incompatible with Genesis 12:4.
entries.commentary:
The arithmetic here is unforgiving and the contradiction is mechanical. Genesis 11:26 — Terah begat Abram at 70. Genesis 11:32 — Terah dies at 205. Subtraction: Abram is 135 when Terah dies. Acts 7:4 — Abram leaves Haran *after* Terah dies. Genesis 12:4 — Abram leaves Haran at 75. 75 does not equal 135.

The standard apologist resolution, which goes back to Augustine and is endorsed by Gleason Archer, takes Genesis 11:26 as a summary statement that doesn't mean Abram was Terah's firstborn. The reasoning: Genesis 11:26 says "Terah lived 70 years and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran" — three sons listed, not all necessarily born when Terah was 70. Abram is listed first because of his theological importance, not birth order. So Abram could actually have been born when Terah was 130, making him 75 when Terah died at 205. The same move is made in Genesis 5 and 10.

This works as a textual maneuver but it's strained. The Hebrew construction of Genesis 11:26 follows the pattern of all the other patriarchal birth notices in chapter 11 — "X lived Y years and begat Z" — and in every other case the begetting age refers to the named child. The apologetic reading has to make Genesis 11:26 uniquely a summary statement while every other case in the chapter is direct. That's special pleading. The harder problem is Acts 7:4 itself. Stephen's speech reflects a tradition (likely from Philo or a similar Second Temple Jewish reading) that explicitly placed Abraham's departure after Terah's death. Stephen and the Genesis 12:4 chronology are operating from different starting assumptions.

The critical consensus, going back to Wellhausen and modern Pentateuchal scholars like Joel Baden, is that the Abraham chronology in Genesis was assembled from P-source genealogies and J-source narrative, and the seams between sources produced the inconsistency. Acts 7 then preserves a separate Hellenistic Jewish tradition that aligned with one possible reading but not with Genesis 12:4 as it stands. Three traditions, no clean fit. Take your pick — but the math is what it is.

answers.answer_explanation: Abram [Abraham] was seventy and five years old when he departed out of Haran. Genesis 12:4

Abraham's father, Terah, was 70 years old when Abram was born.  
				                  
				        And Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram [Abraham]. 
				        Genesis 11:26-32

				        
				      Abraham didn't leave Haran until after Terah died.
				        
				        Our father Abraham ... dwelt in Haran: and from thence, when
				          his father was dead, he removed himself into this land. Acts 7:2-4
				                  
				        
				        And Terah lived to be 205.
				.        
				        And the days of Terah were two hundred and five years; and
				          Terah died in Haran. Genesis 11:32

				          
				          
				          So Abraham was at least 135 years old when he left Haran.

commentary_out.commentary:
The arithmetic is unforgiving and the contradiction is mechanical. Genesis 11:26 — Terah "lived seventy years and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran." Genesis 11:32 — Terah dies at 205. Subtraction yields Abram at 135 when Terah dies. Acts 7:4 — Abram leaves Haran *after* Terah dies. Genesis 12:4 — Abram leaves Haran at 75. Seventy-five does not equal one hundred thirty-five.

The standard apologetic resolution, going back to Augustine and defended by Gleason Archer, treats Genesis 11:26 as a summary notice that does not make Abram the firstborn. The argument: the verse lists three sons, so the begetting age of 70 need only mark when Terah began fathering children, not when Abram specifically was born. Abram is named first for theological prominence, not birth order — so he could have been born when Terah was 130, making him 75 at Terah's death at 205. The same move (named-first ≠ born-first) is applied in the genealogies of Genesis 5 and 10.

The maneuver is grammatically strained. The begetting notices of Genesis 11 follow a rigid, repeated formula — "X lived Y years and begat Z" — and in every single other instance in the chapter the stated age is the age at which the *named* child was born (11:10, 11:12, 11:14, 11:16, 11:18, 11:20, 11:22, 11:24). The harmonization must make 11:26 uniquely a summary statement while treating every parallel notice as direct. That is special pleading driven by the need to reconcile, not by anything in the Hebrew syntax, which is identical across the formulae.

The textual evidence sharpens, rather than dissolves, the problem. At Genesis 11:32 the Samaritan Pentateuch reads Terah's age at death as 145, against the 205 of the Masoretic Text (and the Septuagint) — and 145 is precisely the figure (70 + 75) that makes Abram's departure at 75 fall after his father's death, harmonizing 11:26, 11:32, 12:4, and Acts 7:4 in one stroke. The critical consensus, reflected in Emanuel Tov's standard treatment, is that this is a secondary, harmonizing emendation, exactly the kind of chronological 'correction' the Samaritan tradition is known to make, not the original reading. That matters for the argument: the Masoretic 205 is the harder and earlier reading, and the Samaritan 145 is the fingerprint of an ancient scribe confronting the same contradiction the modern apologist confronts — and 'fixing' the numbers rather than reading 11:26 loosely. The variant does not rescue the inerrantist; it documents that the inconsistency was felt as early as the witnesses themselves.

Acts 7:4 is the deeper issue. Stephen's speech reflects a Second Temple Jewish tradition — paralleled in Philo (*De Migratione Abrahami* 177) — that explicitly placed Abraham's departure from Haran after Terah's death, reading the sequence theologically as a clean break from the father's household. Stephen (or Luke's source) is following that interpretive tradition, which does not align with the plain arithmetic of Genesis 12:4. The critical consensus, from Wellhausen through Joel Baden, is that the Abraham chronology was assembled from the Priestly source's genealogical framework (the precise ages of Genesis 11) and the Yahwistic narrative (the departure at 75 in Genesis 12), and the seam between the sources generated the inconsistency. Acts 7 then preserves a separate Hellenistic-Jewish reading that fit one possible reconstruction but not Genesis 12:4 as transmitted. Three traditions, no clean fit, and an ancient variant that proves the scribes saw the problem too. Verdict: genuine contradiction, with the Samaritan variant confirming early recognition of it.

commentary_out.change_summary: Addressed the audit flag on the Samaritan Pentateuch reading. The SP=145 reading of Gen 11:32 (against MT/LXX 205) is a genuine, well-attested variant, so it was retained rather than removed; the wording was tightened to state it precisely (a documented SP reading of 11:32) and to frame it, per the critical consensus, as a secondary harmonizing emendation rather than the original text. Re-anchored the variant to Emanuel Tov's *Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible* (the standard authority on SP harmonizing corrections) and removed the unverified 'noting the Samaritan variant' gloss from the Hamilton citation. Retained the Philonic background of Stephen's tradition (Migr. Abr. 177), the consistent begetting-formula grammar of Genesis 11, the listed-first-vs-born-first problem, and the P/J source seam.
